title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the table to the paragraph

questions.prompt: Match each holiday with the adjective that judges it best.

options.text: You lie in a hammock and read all afternoon.
You climb, swim and cycle from morning to night.
Fifteen days of the same meal at the same hour.
You come home with photos nobody else has taken.
relaxing
active
monotonous
original

questions.explanation: Reading in a hammock all afternoon rests you, so it is relaxing. Climbing, swimming and cycling from morning to night are sporting activities, so the holiday is active. Fifteen days of the same meal at the same hour is monotonous, because nothing ever changes — the word is stronger than boring. And coming home with photos nobody else has taken is original: the place lies off the usual tourist track.

questions.prompt: A class of 40 pupils said what they would most like to do on a sunny day: a museum 4 votes · the seaside 18 votes · staying at home 2 votes · a football match 7 votes · a picnic in the countryside 9 votes. Put the five outings in the class ranking, from the most chosen to the least chosen.

options.text: the seaside
a picnic in the countryside
a football match
a museum
staying at home

questions.explanation: Reading a table means turning figures into positions: 18 votes for the seaside, 9 for a picnic in the countryside, 7 for a football match, 4 for a museum and 2 for staying at home. The seaside therefore ranks first and staying at home last. Beware of the order in which the figures are printed — survey data is rarely given already sorted, and the ranking is built from the numbers, never from the lines.

questions.prompt: Express the same idea with a habit-in-the-past structure: "Twenty years ago, hardly anybody travelled abroad for the summer; today it is ordinary."

options.text: People hadn't used to travel abroad for the summer.
People didn't used to travel abroad for the summer.
People didn't use travel abroad for the summer.
People didn't use to travel abroad for the summer.

questions.explanation: After the helper "didn't", "used" loses its -d and keeps the "to": People didn't use to travel abroad for the summer. That is the negative of a past habit, and it implies exactly what the sentence says — the habit was missing then and exists now. "didn't used to" marks the past twice, "didn't use travel" drops the "to" that must follow use, and "hadn't used to travel" puts a perfect helper in front of a structure that takes only did.

questions.prompt: A folded sheet left in a hotel room reads: "Our representative will meet you in the lobby at 8 a.m." and is signed "Sunset Travel". Who is writing to whom?

options.text: a customer to a travel agency
a hotel manager to the cleaning staff
a tour guide to a museum
a travel agency to its customers

questions.explanation: "Our representative" is a signature in disguise: the writer is the company that employs the representative, and "Sunset Travel" names it, while the reader is the traveller who will be met in the lobby — a travel agency writing to its customers. A customer would ask for the meeting, not announce it, and neither a manager writing to his staff nor a guide writing to a museum would need to explain where the guests will be picked up.

questions.prompt: Rewrite with "unlike": "My father always camped by the river. I always book a hotel." Which sentence is correct?

options.text: Unlike my father always camped by the river, I always book a hotel.
Unlike my father did, I always book a hotel.
Unlike my father, I always book a hotel.
Unlike of my father, I always book a hotel.

questions.explanation: "Unlike" is a preposition: it takes a noun or a pronoun and nothing else — Unlike my father, I always book a hotel. Putting a whole clause after it turns a preposition into a conjunction, which it never is, and "unlike of" adds a preposition to a word that already is one. Compare with whereas, which does take a clause: My father camped by the river, whereas I book a hotel.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence so that the three parts keep the same structure: "On the island we spent our days swimming in the bay, walking along the cliffs and ___."

options.text: watching the sun go down
watched the sun go down
we watched the sun go down
to watch the sun go down

questions.explanation: The first two parts of the list are "swimming in the bay" and "walking along the cliffs", so the third must keep the same -ing form: watching the sun go down. Repeating one and the same form right through a sentence is parallelism, and every other ending breaks it — a past verb, a new subject, or an infinitive after two -ing forms. Remember that the break nearly always hides in the last item of a list.
